Sample text:
---
The city kept its lost sounds in the basement of the public library. You could go down on a Tuesday and ask for the click your old refrigerator made just before the motor came on. If you filled out a green slip and could approximate the click with your tongue, the clerk would take you to a listening booth.

You weren’t allowed to take the sound home. People had tried.

Mara worked the desk on Tuesdays. Most of her customers were after voices, which the city did not collect. She explained this so often she had stopped trying to make it sound kind.

“We might have the chair he sat in,” she would say. “If it made a noise.”

One afternoon a girl in a bicycle helmet came in with a manila envelope under her arm.

“I lost the sound of a bridge,” she said.

“Which bridge?”

“The footbridge on Mercer. Before they fixed it.”

Mara found the entry: *Mercer footbridge, loose deck board, east end. Two reports of tripping. Removed May 6.* She fetched the sound and set it playing in the booth.

The girl listened three times. The board gave a flat wooden clap, followed by a smaller one as it settled. On the third play the girl put her forehead against the glass.

“Is that it?” Mara asked when she came out.

“Yes. Can I bring my brother?”

“Of course.”

“Can we come after six?”

“We close at five.”

The girl considered this. “He won’t get off the bridge until dark.”

Mara waited for an explanation, but the girl was already sliding the envelope toward her. Inside was a petition with twelve signatures. At the top, in pencil, someone had written: *Please put the noise back.*

The brother was nine. He was blind. Until May 6, he had crossed the footbridge alone on his way home from school. The loose board told him where he was supposed to stop and reach through the rail for the low branch of a willow. From there he could tell which way the wind was moving over the canal. This mattered to him for reasons his sister couldn’t explain.

After the repair, he could still cross the bridge. He just couldn’t find his place on it. He spent his afternoons trying.

“There are other ways to mark a spot,” Mara said.

“I know. I offered to paint it.”

They looked at each other.

“That was a pretty bad offer,” the girl admitted.

Mara called Public Works. The man who answered remembered the board. His father had been one of the people who tripped on it.

“Then you know exactly where it was,” Mara said.

“Sure. But I’m not putting it back.”

He was willing to meet them on Thursday. He arrived with a tape measure and an orange vest over his good shirt. The girl came with her brother, who introduced himself as Leon, and asked them all to stand back because he was in the middle of something.

They stood back. Leon went slowly along the bridge with his cane. Halfway across he stopped, retraced a few steps, and knelt to feel the edge where the boards met the rail.

“Did you find it?” his sister asked.

“No. I found a screw that needs tightening.”

The man from Public Works took a pencil from his pocket.

Watching them, Mara remembered a sound she had never looked for in the basement. When she was small, her mother had taken in sewing and kept a saucer of pins beside the machine. Some nights, long after Mara had been put to bed, she would hear her mother tip the pins from the saucer into a tin. Then the kitchen light would go out. Mara had hated that sound on the nights she couldn’t sleep. It meant the person she was waiting for had finished everything and forgotten to come.

Years later, her mother told her she used to stand outside the bedroom door on those nights, trying to tell from Mara’s breathing whether she was still awake. By then they lived in different states. They had this conversation while Mara was buying onions.

“Would a different noise work?” she asked Leon.

He stood up. “How different?”

The man from Public Works had a socket wrench in his bag. He tapped it against the rail. The rail rang, not beautifully. A woman walking a dog stopped to see what they were doing. Leon tapped the same spot with his cane. It barely made a sound.

“My cane’s not a wrench,” he said.

“No,” the man agreed. He took the rubber cap off the end of the rail and put it back on. Then he asked Leon to show him how he swept his cane when he walked.

The following Thursday there was a little steel plate on the inside of the rail, low enough to catch with a cane, with three raised ribs. Leon passed it once without touching it. On the return trip he drew his cane across all three. It sounded like someone riffling a very short deck of cards.

“Closer to the tree,” he said.

The man moved it two inches.

Mara had brought the old sound in a portable player, though she hadn’t told anyone. She had pictured giving it one last play on the bridge. Now she kept her hands in her coat pockets. Leon’s sister had got bored and was rolling a pill bug gently from one palm to the other. A cyclist rang his bell. Everyone moved except Leon, who was already out of the way.

When Mara got back to the library, she called her mother. She had meant to ask about the tin, but her mother wanted to know how long potatoes lasted after they sprouted. Mara looked it up. They disagreed about what the instructions meant by *firm*.

While they talked, Mara filed the sound of the loose board. On the reverse of the original green slip there was a box marked *Further action*. She wrote, *Leave the screw at the east end alone until Leon shows you which one it is.*

Then she turned off the basement light. Her mother was still on the line, opening drawers, looking for the small knife.
---

The voice is gently observant and restrained: it lets feeling gather through ordinary details rather than spelling out a moral. The lost sounds make memory tangible, but the story’s pathos turns on how a familiar landmark can matter differently to someone navigating by sound and touch. Mara’s own memory of her mother’s pins adds a subdued ache of missed connection. The reader is invited to value attentive accommodation over restoring things exactly as they were.

Its mood is wistful but not elegiac: the old board’s noise is not put back, and the resolution instead makes room for Leon to find his way. The recurring attention to small noises and precise adjustments makes this choice feel central to the story.
